describe all the techniques that Freetoken uses to run MoE models on smaller GPUs.  Consider the latest MoE models that run well on Freetoken.  After that, consider small LLMs, like Hierarchical Reasoning Model and Tiny Recursive Model and how we could build a tiny MoE distilled model from scratch where we could build a small Engram table, and activate a small subset of many tiny experts.  I want to be able to train and run inference on this really scaled-down approach to show step by step how each part works and get some measurable results with reasonable speed on tiny/old hardware.  Maybe even get this to work on systems with 256M RAM and a 0.5 TOPS NPU.

You want to combine three ideas that normally live at very different scales:

FreeToken-style heterogeneous MoE execution — treat RAM, accelerator memory, CPU, and interconnect as a hierarchy rather than requiring all experts to fit on the accelerator.
HRM/TRM-style recursive computation — reuse a very small amount of neural machinery repeatedly instead of buying reasoning depth with many unique layers.
Engram-style conditional memory — move simple memorization/pattern lookup out of the neural network and into a cheap deterministic lookup structure.

I think that combination is unusually well suited to an educational/research system because you can make total parameters, active parameters, active experts, memory traffic, recursion depth, Engram size, and cache size independently adjustable.

1. What FreeToken is really doing

FreeToken's starting observation is straightforward: MoE solves the compute problem but does not automatically solve the storage problem. DeepSeek-V4-Flash, for example, routes each token through only 6 of 256 routed experts in each of 43 layers; roughly 13B of its 284B parameters participate in a token even though the complete expert pool is vastly larger.

So FreeToken does not treat VRAM as "where the model lives."

It treats the machine approximately as:

             FAST / SMALL
       ┌────────────────────┐
       │ GPU VRAM           │
       │                    │
       │ dense/shared       │
       │ model weights      │
       │ KV/state cache     │
       │ HOT EXPERT CACHE   │
       └─────────┬──────────┘
                 │ PCIe
       ┌─────────▼──────────┐
       │ Host RAM           │
       │                    │
       │ COMPLETE EXPERT    │
       │ POOL               │
       └─────────┬──────────┘
                 │
       ┌─────────▼──────────┐
       │ SSD / checkpoint   │
       └────────────────────┘
             SLOW / LARGE

Non-expert weights normally remain GPU resident, while host RAM is the authoritative copy of the routed experts. Everything left in VRAM becomes an elastic expert cache shared across layers. A cache entry represents a complete (layer, expert) rather than independent tensor fragments.

That separation is the fundamental trick.

The FreeToken techniques
Technique	What it accomplishes	Tiny-model analogue
Sparse MoE routing	Only k << E experts execute	32–64 experts, top-1/top-2
Host-resident expert pool	Total model can exceed VRAM	Flash/DRAM holds all experts
Global GPU expert cache	Hot experts execute locally	SRAM/NPU memory expert cache
Routing-aware LRU	Cache follows actual workload	Measure/cache recent experts
Full-layer prefill streaming	Hides bulk weight movement	DMA next expert bank
Double buffering	Transfer N+1 while computing N	Two scratch buffers
CPU/GPU hybrid execution	Misses can execute without transfer	CPU + NPU cooperation
q* scheduling	Chooses transfer vs CPU dynamically	Scheduler based on measured bandwidth
Quantized experts	Reduces RAM and transfer traffic	INT8/INT4 experts
CUDA-graph-compatible routing	Removes host dispatch overhead	Static compiled dispatch graph
CPU SIMD + dequantization	Makes CPU miss path bandwidth-efficient	SIMD fallback kernels
Elastic VRAM allocation	Trades expert cache against KV memory	Dynamic SRAM allocation
FTW expert-bank layout	Avoids runtime repacking	Native packed embedded format
Fast bootstrap	Load directly into final representation	mmap/direct DMA packed weights
Semantic prefix/state caching	Avoids recomputation after context edits	Recursive-state snapshots
Radix KV prefix cache	Reuses common prefixes	Optional small prefix cache
Hardware calibration	Measures real RAM/PCIe behavior	Benchmark flash/DRAM/NPU/CPU

The especially important ones for your project are the expert hierarchy, LRU, hybrid miss handling, packed expert format, quantization, and measurement-based scheduling.

2. Prefill and decode are deliberately treated differently

This is one of FreeToken's more interesting decisions.

During generation, MoE routing is sparse. But during a long prompt, thousands of input tokens collectively tend to touch most experts. FreeToken found that trying to fetch individual experts on demand during prefill therefore doesn't buy much.

Instead it allocates two complete expert-layer buffers. While the GPU executes layer L, it streams the experts for layer L+1. The buffers swap roles.

Conceptually:

time ─────────────────────────────────────────────>

GPU:     compute L0 | compute L1 | compute L2 | compute L3
PCIe:       load L1 |    load L2 |    load L3 | load L4
             ^ overlap ^

buffer A:     L0          L2          L4
buffer B:          L1          L3

On an RTX 5090 the paper reports streaming a 64.4-GB expert pool at roughly 52.7 GB/s during an 8192-token prefill; removing the second buffer reduced throughput materially as prompt size increased.

Your tiny implementation should reproduce this experiment even if the buffers contain only tens or hundreds of KB.

That makes the effect visible rather than merely theoretical.

3. Decode becomes an expert-cache problem

Decode is the opposite.

For one token:

router
   |
   +---- expert 3  ---- cache hit
   +---- expert 17 ---- cache hit
   +---- expert 41 ---- MISS

FreeToken uses temporal locality: adjacent tokens frequently select overlapping experts.

So instead of deciding at startup that "experts 0–31 belong on the GPU," it uses an LRU cache whose contents continuously follow actual routing decisions.

That sounds obvious in hindsight, but it is fundamentally different from static offload.

Your demonstration should expose this explicitly:

Token    Selected experts    cache hit/miss
-----    ----------------    --------------
102        3,17                 H,H
103        3,22                 H,M
104       17,22                 H,H
105        3,41                 H,M

Then graph:

cache hit rate
bytes transferred/token
tokens/sec

against cache capacity.

This could become one of the best demonstrations in the project.

4. FreeToken's cleverest mechanism: q*

Suppose a layer needs four experts that aren't in VRAM.

A simplistic system has two choices:

A: transfer all four → GPU
B: execute all four → CPU

FreeToken instead does both simultaneously.

It measures:

B_P: pinned host→GPU transfer bandwidth
B_H: host-memory expert processing bandwidth

and approximately chooses

$$ q^* = m {B_P \over B_H} $$

where m is the number of missing experts.

So:

               4 missing experts
                      |
          ┌───────────┴──────────┐
          │                      │
    transfer/cache           CPU execute
       expert 41             expert 52
                             expert 59
                             expert 63
          │                      │
        GPU                    CPU
          └───────────┬──────────┘
                      │
                  sum output

Both outputs are exact partial MoE outputs; this is not an approximation of the model.

That distinction is important.

The scheduler is approximating the best resource allocation, not the neural computation.

FreeToken now provides ft bench bw specifically to measure these characteristics on the target machine rather than guessing them from specifications.

For your system I'd generalize this to:

$$ q^* = f(B_\text{flash},B_\text{RAM},B_\text{DMA}, B_\text{CPU},B_\text{NPU}) $$

That might actually become a genuinely interesting embedded-systems research result.

5. FreeToken also removes the scheduler from the critical path

There is a less glamorous but important implementation trick.

FreeToken keeps routing/cache decisions compatible with CUDA graph execution. Routing-dependent work—deduplicating experts, determining hits/misses, choosing LRU victims and translating logical expert numbers into physical slots—runs inside fixed graph machinery rather than bouncing repeatedly through Python/host scheduling.

Its CPU side likewise uses persistent native worker threads pinned to physical cores, SIMD kernels, and in-kernel dequantization.

For a 0.5-TOPS NPU, this lesson may matter even more than on CUDA:

Do not make tiny expert dispatches expensive.

A 30-µs neural expert isn't useful if selecting and launching it costs 100 µs.

That argues strongly for a restricted routing scheme that can be ahead-of-time compiled.

6. Quantization helps twice

FreeToken currently supports combinations including BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and MXFP4 depending on model/backend.

For an offloaded MoE model quantization gives two benefits:

$$ \text{smaller weights} \Rightarrow \begin{cases} \text{more experts fit in cache}\\ \text{less data crosses PCIe} \end{cases} $$

That second property is particularly important.

For your embedded system, INT4 expert weights may therefore be more useful than INT4 dense weights.

The shared network can initially remain INT8 while experts become INT4.

7. FTW is also worth copying conceptually

FreeToken normalizes architecture-specific experts into expert banks keyed by something equivalent to:

expert_id = layer * experts_per_layer + expert

and FTW stores the checkpoint already arranged that way. Loading can therefore read aligned blocks directly into their runtime host representation rather than loading a generic checkpoint and rearranging hundreds of GB afterward.

It also populates host memory before pinning it, avoiding needless zero/fault work on enormous pinned allocations.

Your format might deliberately be extremely simple:

TinyMoE file
├── header
├── tokenizer
├── shared weights
├── routers
├── engram
├── expert-index
├── expert-0000
├── expert-0001
├── ...
└── expert-N

Each expert should be independently DMA-able.

That would make experiments with HDD/SSD/SPI-flash/RAM/external SRAM unusually straightforward.

8. The currently interesting FreeToken models

FreeToken's current known-good model list has moved beyond its original three headline models. The documentation now lists DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.2, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Qwen3.6/3.5 MoE, Qwen3-MoE, GPT-OSS, Gemma-4, MiniMax-M2.5 and Muse-Glimmer variants.

The headline results from the paper remain particularly informative:

Model	Why interesting
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B	Small active footprint; FreeToken reports 77–83 tok/s on RTX 5090
DeepSeek-V4-Flash	284B total, ~13B active; 22–25 tok/s on RTX 5090
GLM-5.2	753B total; demonstrated on a single workstation GPU
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next	Newer architecture, particularly interesting for your memory idea

Those headline performance results come from the FreeToken evaluation.

And there is a rather striking connection to your Engram idea: FreeToken's current model documentation says Qwen3.8-Flash-Next uses a 47.7-GiB PLE n-gram table pinned in host RAM.

That is almost a giant-scale version of one component we're proposing to miniaturize.

9. Now combine this with HRM/TRM

There is an important distinction first:

HRM and TRM are not tiny general-purpose LLMs.

HRM's original model was 27M parameters and obtained striking results on structured reasoning tasks using recurrence and two interacting modules operating at different timescales rather than a deep stack of unique layers.

TRM simplifies the concept dramatically: essentially a tiny recurrent network repeatedly updates a latent state and candidate answer. The original TRM work uses about 7M parameters and only two neural layers.

Some follow-up results also suggest caution about interpreting the headline ARC numbers: performance depends substantially on task conditioning, augmentation, sampling/voting and test-time compute.

But that doesn't weaken the architectural lesson relevant here:

Reasoning depth does not necessarily require parameter depth.

That is exactly what we want.

10. I would build a Recursive Tiny MoE

Rather than:

Transformer layer 0
Transformer layer 1
Transformer layer 2
...
Transformer layer 24

I'd build:

             ┌───────────────────────┐
tokens ─────►│ embedding + Engram    │
             └──────────┬────────────┘
                        ▼
              ┌───────────────────┐
              │ shared recurrent  │◄──────────────┐
              │ reasoning block   │               │
              └───────┬───────────┘               │
                      │                           │
                  router                          │
                 /  |  \                          │
                /   |   \                         │
            expert expert expert                  │
                \   |   /                         │
                 combine                          │
                      │                           │
                update state ─────────────────────┘
                      │
                after R cycles
                      ▼
                    LM head

Unique parameter count stays tiny.

Effective computational depth becomes adjustable.

11. A concrete first architecture

I'd start approximately here:

Component	V0
Vocabulary	4,096
d_model	256
Physical recurrent blocks	4
Recurrences	1–8 selectable
Experts/block	32
Active experts	top-2
Expert hidden width	128
Attention	GQA or very small causal attention
Engram	hashed 2/3/4-gram
Engram slots	65,536
Engram value width	32
Training precision	BF16/FP16
Deployment shared weights	INT8
Deployment experts	INT8 → INT4
Engram	INT8

A gated expert roughly needs:

$$ 3\times256\times128 \approx 98K $$

parameters.

Therefore:

$$ 98K\times32\times4 \approx 12.6M $$

expert parameters total.

Add embeddings, attention, routers and projections and you're probably still around 15–20M parameters.

At INT4:

20M parameters × 0.5 byte ≈ 10 MB

before scales and metadata.

That is almost comically small relative to 256 MB.

So we can afford to increase the experiment substantially later.

12. And this is where "many experts" becomes interesting

Suppose instead we have:

4 blocks
64 experts/block
top-2

We have:

256 experts physically present
  8 expert executions per recurrent sweep

So only:

$$ 8/256 = 3.1\% $$

of the expert population is active during one pass.

If we perform four recurrent iterations:

iteration 0 → experts {7,19,...}
iteration 1 → experts {7,22,...}
iteration 2 → experts {4,22,...}
iteration 3 → experts {4,31,...}

we get something especially interesting:

expert routing over reasoning time

not merely routing over transformer depth.

That could show genuine emergent specialization.

For example:

expert 7   → syntax
expert 12  → arithmetic
expert 22  → identifier relationships
expert 31  → answer refinement

We should not force those meanings.

We should instrument the model and discover whether such specialization develops.

13. Add the Engram as another sparse axis

DeepSeek describes Engram as complementary to MoE:

MoE = conditional computation
Engram = conditional memory

Engram performs deterministic N-gram addressing and retrieves learned memory values in essentially O(1), avoiding the need for neural layers to repeatedly reconstruct common token patterns. DeepSeek also emphasizes that deterministic addressing makes very large tables naturally offloadable.

Our tiny version could be delightfully simple.

For recent tokens:

"for" "(" "i"

compute:

h2 = hash("(" ,"i")       % table_size
h3 = hash("for","(","i")  % table_size

lookup:

E2[h2]
E3[h3]

then:

engram = projection(E2 + E3)

and combine:

$$ h'_t = h_t + g_t\cdot E_\text{ngram} $$

where g is a learned gate.

Initially:

65536 entries
× 32 dimensions
× INT8
≈ 2 MB

Beautifully manageable.

14. There is a useful negative result to keep in mind

A recent independent experiment applying Engram-like tables to small 0.5B–4B models found substantial perplexity improvements but essentially no consistent gain on HellaSwag, PIQA or ARC-Challenge.

That makes your experiment more interesting, not less.

We can directly measure:

                         Perplexity    reasoning    memory      speed
Dense baseline
+ recurrence
+ MoE
+ Engram
+ recurrence + MoE
+ MoE + Engram
+ all three

Instead of assuming that Engram must help.

15. The experimental progression I would use

This is where I think your project can become much more valuable than simply "another tiny LLM."

Stage	Architecture	Question
0	dense tiny transformer	Baseline
1	recurrent shared layers	Does repeated compute replace parameters?
2	dense + Engram	Does external memory improve PPL/tasks?
3	top-1 MoE	Can experts specialize?
4	top-2 MoE	Is quality worth doubled active compute?
5	recurrent MoE	Does expert selection change during reasoning?
6	recurrent MoE + Engram	Do memory and compute sparsity complement each other?
7	quantized	What quality is lost at INT8/INT4?
8	constrained expert cache	What does cache size do?
9	CPU/NPU hybrid	Can FreeToken-style scheduling help?
10	256-MB target	Can the complete architecture survive embedded deployment?

Every stage produces a measurable result.

That is considerably better pedagogically than starting with the final architecture.

16. Distillation: "from scratch" still makes sense

I would interpret "distilled from scratch" as:

Initialize the tiny model randomly, but train it partly from targets produced by a capable teacher.

We're not pruning or compressing an existing network.

We create our own:

tokenizer
architecture
router
experts
Engram
recursive computation

from scratch.

Then a larger teacher generates:

input → teacher output

and, where practical:

teacher token probability distribution

Student objective:

$$ L = \alpha L_\text{token} +\beta L_\text{KD} +\gamma L_\text{router} +\delta L_\text{balance} $$

Potentially later:

$$ +\epsilon L_\text{recurrence} $$

where intermediate recursive states are rewarded for progressively improving the answer.

We don't need a frontier teacher. A modest local 1B–7B model can generate vastly better training labels than our ~20M student.

17. Start with a constrained domain

I would not initially train it to be a general chatbot.

That confounds too many things.

I'd use a mixture like:

natural language
simple code
arithmetic
sequence transformations
logic puzzles
small algorithms
structured text

with synthetic data heavily represented.

Why?

Because then we can actually see whether experts specialize.

Imagine a router eventually producing:

arithmetic → experts 3,17
Rust syntax → experts 8,26
English prose → experts 2,14
sequence reasoning → experts 21,31

That's an educational result you can inspect.

18. Metrics should go far beyond perplexity

For every run I'd record:

Neural	Systems
validation loss	tokens/sec
perplexity	bytes/token
task accuracy	RAM peak
teacher/student KL	accelerator RAM
active params/token	expert cache hit rate
router entropy	expert transfers/token
expert load balance	CPU vs NPU work
expert specialization	energy/token
accuracy vs recursion	latency/token
Engram contribution	Engram collisions
Engram gate magnitude	cache reuse distance

FreeToken demonstrates why this matters: systems characteristics can dominate performance even when the mathematical model remains identical.

19. Your 256-MB / 0.5-TOPS target is plausible — with qualifications

Inference: absolutely plausible for this tiny architecture.

Training the complete system on-device: much less attractive.

A 20M-parameter model may require only about:

INT8   ~20 MB
INT4   ~10 MB

for deployed weights.

But Adam-style training might require roughly:

weights
gradients
master weights
first moment
second moment
activations

and quickly exceed 256 MB.

So I'd separate:

training machine
    ↓
quantized packed checkpoint
    ↓
256-MB inference device

and then optionally support limited on-device learning:

router adaptation
Engram updates
small expert fine-tuning
last-layer training

That would itself be an interesting experiment.

20. 0.5 TOPS probably isn't the real limit

For this design the limiting resource may be:

memory bandwidth and dispatch latency, not TOPS.

Suppose a token touches only ~1–3M parameters through recurrent sparse execution.

Even at several recurrent steps that's nowhere near a 0.5-TOPS theoretical arithmetic ceiling.

But if each tiny expert causes:

flash read
DMA setup
NPU submission
synchronization

the accelerator may spend more time launching experts than multiplying matrices.

Therefore I would design the NPU architecture around expert bundles rather than arbitrary individual networks.

For example:

expert-bank-0 = experts 0..7
expert-bank-1 = experts 8..15
...

and make the router's scheduling granular enough to suit the actual NPU compiler.

21. A more radical option: experts as low-rank deltas

For the smallest machine, I'd also test:

            shared FFN
                +
       selected expert delta

rather than completely separate FFNs.

Each expert becomes:

$$ \Delta W_e = A_eB_e $$

with rank perhaps 4 or 8.

Then you can afford hundreds of experts.

Example:

d = 256
rank = 8

expert parameters
≈ 2 × 256 × 8
= 4096

So:

256 experts ≈ 1M parameters

per expert location.

That gives you genuinely large expert populations while remaining tiny.

This may actually be a better fit for the 0.5-TOPS NPU because the big shared matrix remains static and accelerator-friendly.

22. My preferred eventual architecture

I would call the conceptual design something like µMoE-RM for now:

                   token IDs
                      │
            ┌─────────▼────────┐
            │ token embedding  │
            └─────────┬────────┘
                      │
       recent tokens ─┼─────────────┐
                      │             │
                      │       ┌─────▼─────┐
                      │       │  Engram   │
                      │       │ 2/3/4gram │
                      │       └─────┬─────┘
                      │             │
                 ┌────▼─────────────▼──┐
                 │ recurrent core      │◄──────┐
                 │ attention/state     │       │
                 └────────┬────────────┘       │
                          │                    │
                    ┌─────▼─────┐              │
                    │  router   │              │
                    └─────┬─────┘              │
                          │ top-k               │
                    ┌─────▼─────┐              │
             RAM/   │ expert    │              │
             flash──┤ cache     │              │
                    └─────┬─────┘              │
                          │                    │
             ┌────────────┼────────────┐       │
             │            │            │       │
          expert       expert       expert     │
             │            │            │       │
             └────────────┼────────────┘       │
                          │                    │
                     combine                   │
                          │                    │
                     state update ─────────────┘
                          │
                      LM head

It has three independent kinds of sparsity:

$$ \boxed{ \text{parameter sharing} + \text{conditional compute} + \text{conditional memory} } $$

namely:

recurrence → temporal parameter reuse

MoE       → compute sparsity

Engram    → memory lookup sparsity

FreeToken then adds a fourth:

expert cache → residency sparsity

That is a remarkably elegant little research system.

23. It also fits your older hardware progression unusually well

I would actually develop it downward:

RTX 3090 / 5060
       │
       ▼
normal training + profiling
       │
       ▼
RTX 3060 / P40
       │
       ▼
CPU-only old Xeon
       │
       ▼
small SBC
       │
       ▼
LicheeRV/SG2002-class
256 MB + ~0.5 TOPS NPU

At every step, constrain the previous system artificially:

64 MB expert cache
32 MB
16 MB
8 MB
...

before moving to the real hardware.

Then an embedded failure isn't mysterious—you already know approximately where the knee in the curve should occur.

The experiment I would build first

I would resist starting with language generation.

Build a ~5–10M parameter recurrent MoE, perhaps 16 experts with top-2, and train it on synthetic transformations plus tiny text.

Give it a 64K × 32 ≈ 2-MB Engram.

Then build a visual/instrumented runtime showing:

current token
↓
Engram addresses + retrieved values
↓
recursive iteration 1
    router → experts 3,7
recursive iteration 2
    router → experts 3,12
recursive iteration 3
    router → experts 9,12
↓
prediction

alongside:

expert cache
┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
│ E3 │ E7 │E12 │ E9 │... │
└────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘

hits     7
misses   2
loads    1
CPU      1
NPU      8

Once that works, scale the number of experts upward while keeping active parameters nearly constant.

That gives you a very clean experimental question:

$$ \textbf{How much model capacity can we add without adding proportional compute?} $$

Then add the second question:

$$ \textbf{How much of that capacity actually needs to reside near the accelerator?} $$

And finally the Engram question:

$$ \textbf{How much memorization can be removed from neural computation altogether?} $$

Those three questions connect TRM/HRM → MoE → Engram → FreeToken → your 256-MB NPU target much more coherently than simply trying to shrink an existing LLM.

I think this is strong enough to justify its own experimental repo rather than being merely another sw-mlpl demonstration: the repo could progressively implement Dense → Recursive → MoE → Engram → Cached MoE → Hybrid CPU/NPU, with every stage retaining comparable benchmarks and trace visualizations.

what would we call this new repo?

Given the repo's purpose—a small, inspectable experimental model that combines recursive reasoning, sparse MoE, Engram memory, and FreeToken-inspired memory hierarchy—I'd avoid naming it after any one of those techniques. The interesting thing is the combination.

My strongest candidates:

Name	Why it works
tiny-moe-lab	Immediately understandable; emphasizes experimentation
micro-moe	Short, memorable, emphasizes extreme scaling-down
recursive-moe	Captures perhaps the most novel architectural combination
sparse-reasoner	Describes the goal rather than implementation
tiny-sparse-reasoner	More explicit about scale
micro-reasoner	Nice if MoE/Engram are implementation details
tiny-conditional-model	Captures conditional compute + memory
micro-moe-reasoner	Descriptive without being too long
tiny-moe-research	Serious/academic sounding, but generic
moe-microscope	Excellent if education/visualization is central
I particularly like moe-microscope

It fits what we're actually proposing better than tiny-moe-lab.

The project isn't merely trying to create the smallest useful MoE. It's intended to let someone look inside one:

token
  ↓
Engram lookup ─────────► inspect
  ↓
recurrent state ───────► inspect
  ↓
router ────────────────► inspect
  ↓
expert selection ──────► inspect
  ↓
expert cache ──────────► inspect
  ↓
CPU/NPU scheduling ────► inspect
  ↓
prediction

And experiments can progressively turn mechanisms on:

dense
  → recursive
  → MoE
  → recursive MoE
  → + Engram
  → + quantization
  → + expert caching
  → + heterogeneous execution
  → tiny hardware

That makes moe-microscope a good description of the project's educational purpose rather than just its architecture.

It also connects nicely with the "ML microscope" concept we've discussed for your visualization work without tying the repository to sw-MLPL itself.

Another direction: micro-moe

If you expect this to become more serious model research than educational visualization, I'd choose:

micro-moe

It gives you room for:

Micro-MoE is an experimental framework for training and deploying extremely small mixture-of-experts models using recursive computation, sparse learned experts, associative Engram memory, quantization, and hierarchical expert storage.

Then the project's named model could be something different:

µMoE-R — recursive Micro-MoE
µMoE-E — + Engram
µMoE-X — heterogeneous/offloaded version

That gives you clean experimental nomenclature:

µMoE-D    dense baseline
µMoE-R    recursive
µMoE-S    sparse experts
µMoE-RE   recursive + Engram
µMoE-RSE  recursive + sparse + Engram

Though I'd probably avoid getting too acronym-heavy until experiments justify the distinctions.

My preference

I'd use:

Repo: moe-microscope
Building mixture-of-experts models small enough to understand.

with the first actual architecture called:

MicroMoE

That separates the research/teaching environment from the model being studied.

It also leaves moe-microscope free to compare MicroMoE against dense, recurrent, TRM-like, Engram, cached/offloaded, and other architectures rather than prematurely defining the repo as one particular model.

content.content:
# demo-ml-microscope

Executable sw-MLPL lessons that expose semantically named intermediate values
as a recorded timeline. The goal is an ML microscope: read the algorithm in
MLPL, change it, run it, and inspect how arrays, parameters, gradients, and
metrics evolve without replacing the lesson with a bespoke Rust simulator.

The project starts from current public sw-MLPL behavior. In particular,
`emit_frame(name, step, value)` already streams a whole numeric tensor and
returns that value unchanged. The first implementation milestone will test how
far a small MLPL facade over that primitive can go before requesting any core
or native work.

## Ownership boundary

- This repository owns ML concepts, lesson sequencing, observation names,
  explanations, numeric evidence, and `.mlpl` applications.
- [`demo-mlpl-libraries`](../demo-mlpl-libraries) is the future home for a
  domain-neutral observation helper only after three unrelated lessons prove
  its API. This repository will then consume a revision-pinned vendored copy.
- [`demo-extensions`](../demo-extensions) is the future home for the preferred
  full-featured Rust/Yew WASM microscope. Its existing native graphics support
  may later provide optional desktop/3-D views. Neither renderer may contain
  algorithm-specific visualizers.
- [`sw-mlpl`](../sw-mlpl) should change only for measured language-wide gaps,
  such as a versioned frame protocol or generic browser Explorer host that
  cannot be expressed downstream.

Sibling repositories are read-only from this project. Exact work requests and
acceptance criteria are recorded in
[`docs/cross-repo-handoffs.md`](docs/cross-repo-handoffs.md).

## Planned learning path

The first three forcing-function lessons are deliberately different:

1. matrix multiplication for concept-by-concept stepping;
2. linear regression for iterative parameters, gradients, and metrics;
3. K-means for named assignment/update phases.

## First visual microscope

MM01 is now executable. It follows one output cell from its selected row and
column through component products and partial sums, then compares the complete
derived matrix with native `matmul`.

![Matrix multiplication microscope showing the active row, column, products, partial sums, and completed output cell](assets/previews/matrix-microscope.svg)

```sh
just matrix             # run MLPL and check the generated visual
just matrix-recording   # prove live SSE equals the Yew fixture
```

Read the [MM01 lesson guide](docs/matrix-microscope.md) or inspect the
[standalone MLPL source](demos/matrix_microscope.mlpl). The committed
[recording fixture](fixtures/yew/matrix-run-v0.json) is the first integration
input for the planned Rust/Yew viewer in `demo-extensions`.

See [graphics and animation options](docs/graphics-options.md) for the Yew,
CSS, SVG, GIF, WebP, video, native-renderer, README, and accessibility decisions,
including exact commands for viewing the current deliverable.

## Gradient descent microscope

LR01 exposes an entire two-parameter learning loop: predictions, residuals,
mean squared loss, analytic gradient, parameters, and trajectory. Eight updates
fit four exact points on `y=2x+1`; five bounded checkpoints are retained for
playback.

![Linear regression data and fitted line beside falling loss and the parameter trajectory](assets/previews/linear-regression-microscope.svg)

```sh
just regression             # run MLPL and check the generated visual
just regression-recording   # prove live SSE equals the Yew fixture
```

Read the [LR01 lesson guide](docs/linear-regression-microscope.md), the
[standalone MLPL source](demos/linear_regression_microscope.mlpl), or the
[recording fixture](fixtures/yew/linear-regression-run-v0.json).

## K-means phase microscope

KM01 separates assignment from update instead of hiding both operations in one
iteration. Six fixed 2-D points converge after two updates, with squared
distances, labels, objective, centroids, cluster counts, and centroid movement
available as exact retained observations.

![K-means points and centroids alongside exact assignment and update phase evidence](assets/previews/kmeans-microscope.svg)

```sh
just kmeans             # run MLPL and check the generated visual
just kmeans-recording   # prove live SSE equals the Yew fixture
```

Read the [KM01 lesson guide](docs/kmeans-microscope.md), the
[standalone MLPL source](demos/kmeans_microscope.mlpl), or the
[recording fixture](fixtures/yew/kmeans-run-v0.json).

## Interactive viewer status

The offline Rust/Yew viewer has been delivered in `../demo-extensions` with
Previous/Next/Play/Pause/Seek over MM01 and LR01. This repo contains its
revision-pinned
[Rust/Yew viewer handoff](docs/yew-viewer-handoff.md), shared
[recording schema](fixtures/yew/recording-schema-v0.json), and checked
[fixture index](fixtures/yew/index-v1.json). Run:

```sh
just yew-handoff
```

KM01 is now the third producer fixture. The next `../demo-extensions` agent
should vendor the indexed producer revision and prove that the same generic UI
renders its assignment/update phases without K-means-specific Rust.

Only after those share a stable observation vocabulary will the project move
through MLP forward/backward state, PCA, attention, a tiny language model,
LoRA, and Engram. Existing sw-MLPL model and visualization primitives remain
the implementation; this repository does not build another transformer in
Rust.

Read the [architecture](docs/architecture.md), measured
[observation contract](docs/observation-contract.md),
[delivery plan](docs/plan.md), [saga queue](docs/sagas.md), and
[capability ledger](docs/sw-mlpl-blockers.md) before implementing a lesson.
The original design discussion is retained in
[`docs/research.txt`](docs/research.txt).

## Development process

Work is divided into durable Agentrail steps. In each fresh session run
`agentrail next`, then `agentrail begin`; implement only that step; run focused
tests and the precommit gate; commit source and `.agentrail/` metadata; and
only then run `agentrail complete`. [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) contains the full
repository protocol.

The foundation gate is:

```sh
just check
```

It checks repository structure, documentation links, the generated Agentrail
briefing, canonical MLPL style, native mlplunit tests, public error diagnostics,
and the loopback SSE frame contract. Future lesson steps must extend the gate
with their focused demos and acceptance tests.
`sw-checklist` is reserved for Rust work in `../demo-extensions` and is not a
gate for this MLPL repository.

## Current status

The measured `emit_frame` contract and the matrix, regression, and K-means
microscopes are complete. All three recordings are pinned in the checked Yew
handoff. The next local task is reviewing their shared observation mechanisms;
live evaluator control and reverse execution remain outside this milestone.

## Completed: foundation contract

Install Agentrail process rules; match peer copyright and MIT license; create
the README, architecture, plan, ownership handoffs, capability ledger, and
documentation-only `just check` gate.

Acceptance: generated instructions are current, peer license files compare
byte-for-byte, local documentation links resolve, the local MLPL/documentation
gate passes, and no sibling worktree is modified.

## Completed: measured emit-frame contract

Add native mlplunit/tool-selection infrastructure and probe current
`emit_frame` behavior: identity return, disconnected no-op, accepted numeric
shapes, name/step behavior, event ordering, and connect-path payload. Freeze a
small recorded-observation contract from measured evidence.

Accepted: four native mlplunit identity/rank/boundary tests, two public error
fixtures, and a live loopback SSE probe now run under `just check`. The measured
contract is in `docs/observation-contract.md`.

## Completed: matrix concept stepping

Implement matrix multiplication in readable MLPL, exposing inputs, row/column,
products, partial sums, and result while independently asserting the output.

Accepted: MM01 emits eight literal observations over five steps, derives the
exact 2-by-2 result, checks native `matmul` parity, generates a freshness-checked
SVG, and matches the committed budgeted Yew fixture over live SSE.

## Completed: linear-regression timeline

Implement bounded deterministic linear regression with prediction, residual,
loss, gradient, parameter, and trajectory observations.

Accepted: LR01 performs eight explicit analytic-gradient updates, retains five
checkpoints with 32 observations, reduces MSE from 21 below 0.0004, generates a
freshness-checked SVG, and matches its bounded Yew fixture over live SSE.

## Completed locally and in sibling: Yew interactive viewer handoff

The shared schema, hash-pinned fixture index, two consumer recordings, pure
model boundaries, reducer semantics, generic views, accessibility behavior,
native/browser acceptance cases, and build/run/deploy contract are frozen in
`docs/yew-viewer-handoff.md`.

The independently authorized `../demo-extensions` agent delivered the offline
Rust/Yew app at commits `2ef0e33` and `3ecd025`, including its Rust checks and
Agentrail closeout. Live browser-to-server execution remains a later layer.

## Completed: K-means phases

KM01 implements bounded deterministic K-means assignment/update phases. Five
frames and fourteen observations establish grouping by numeric step plus
slash-separated semantic prefix, with stable call order and no new protocol
field or algorithm-specific renderer.

## Future

Review the three consumers and hand off a reusable MLPL observation helper.
The `demo-extensions` agent should first vendor KM01 into its generic viewer.
Then add MLP forward/backward, PCA, attention, tiny LM, LoRA, and Engram.
Optional native graphics remain a separate renderer handoff.
=== plan.md ===
# ML microscope delivery plan

## Outcome

Build executable sw-MLPL lessons whose own semantically named intermediate
values form a recorded, inspectable timeline. A learner can read and modify the
MLPL algorithm, rerun it, and review how its state changes without a bespoke
Rust implementation of each ML concept.

MLPL owns concepts and application semantics. Hosts render generic observed
values and manage playback or interaction. Work moves upstream only after a
downstream executable probe proves that current public behavior blocks a
general contract.

## Evidence and current constraints

- `emit_frame(name, step, x)` streams a whole numeric tensor through the
  connect-mode metric sink, returns `x`, and is a no-op when disconnected.
- sw-MLPL already provides arrays, named axes, autograd, model helpers,
  attention extraction, traces, SVG plots, browser/WASM execution, and SSE.
- Current frame events carry a name, numeric step, shape, and numeric values;
  they do not yet constitute a versioned multi-observation lesson protocol.
- `demo-extensions` already proves arrays, records, handles, a parked-main
  Port architecture, and headless/native rendering tests.
- `demo-mlpl-libraries` already proves revision-pinned, hash-verified source
  vendoring for reusable MLPL modules.
- Recorded rewind is host-side browsing. Reverse evaluation and synchronous
  browser checkpoints are deliberately outside the first milestone.

## Architecture rule

```text
demo-ml-microscope (.mlpl concepts and lessons)
          |
          +-- repeated domain-neutral helpers --> demo-mlpl-libraries
          |
          +-- generic native UI requirement ----> demo-extensions (Rust)
          |
          `-- proven language-wide blocker ------> sw-mlpl
```

Rust may define generic observation envelopes, bounded retention, tensor
inspectors, renderers, timelines, transports, and playback controls. It must
not define `TransformerVisualizer`, `PcaVisualizer`, `KMeansVisualizer`, or
other algorithm-specific semantics.

## Saga 1: foundation and measured contract

1. Establish Agentrail instructions, licensing, project README, repository
   checks, architecture, cross-repository ownership, and an evidence-backed
   capability ledger.
2. Probe `emit_frame` across the supported interpreter/connect path and freeze
   the smallest recorded-observation contract: names, steps, grouping, numeric
   shapes, fidelity, ordering, budgets, errors, and disconnected behavior.
3. Add root mlplunit/tool selection/style infrastructure and one tiny fixture
   proving the current public API without adding Rust or changing siblings.

Exit: `just check` passes from a clean checkout and documentation distinguishes
supported, awkward, and blocked behavior using executable evidence.

## Saga 2: pure-MLPL proof of concept

After the first two lessons, prioritize the implementation-ready Rust/Yew
viewer handoff so interactive playback can proceed in `demo-extensions` before
the K-means lesson. This ordering change does not authorize sibling edits from
this repository.

1. Implement matrix multiplication as concept stepping: inputs, selected row
   and column, products, partial sums, and completed output.
2. Implement two-parameter linear regression/gradient descent with data,
   predictions, residuals, loss, gradients, parameters, and trajectory frames.
3. Implement K-means with explicit initial, assignment, and centroid-update
   phases, forcing a clean convention for multiple observations per step.
4. Build a deterministic recorded-timeline artifact and a dependency-free
   textual/static viewer sufficient for acceptance; browser and native hosts
   remain optional consumers of the same data.

Exit: three unrelated lessons use the same small observation helpers; retained
state is bounded; numeric/text evidence exists independently of visuals.

## Saga 3: reusable MLPL observation library

1. Review the helpers after three consumers and freeze only domain-neutral
   functions such as observe-at, metric, note, and bounded summaries.
2. Write a producer contract and a separately actionable extraction handoff for
   `demo-mlpl-libraries`, including prefixes, tests, catalog metadata, install
   provenance, and migration order.
3. After that sibling change is independently delivered, vendor the immutable
   library revision here and prove hash-checked consumption. Do not couple this
   repo to an adjacent working tree at runtime.

Exit: this repository consumes a pinned library; lesson semantics remain local.

## Saga 4: deeper ML learning path

Add capability-supported lessons in prerequisite order: vector/shape
inspection, MLP forward pass, explicit backward gradients, PCA, attention,
tiny language model, LoRA, and Engram. Each lesson names shapes, tolerance,
claim boundaries, and the exact supported/awkward/blocking capabilities it
exercises. Transformer work reuses sw-MLPL's model implementation; it does not
implement a second transformer in Rust.

Exit: the learning path reaches a small real model while remaining readable,
bounded, deterministic, and executable as MLPL.

## Saga 5: generic hosts after protocol proof

1. Specify a versioned, renderer-neutral observation/timeline interchange from
   measured artifacts, including budgets and malformed-input behavior.
2. Hand off a full-featured generic Rust/Yew WASM microscope to
   `demo-extensions`. It consumes ordered SSE frames, owns bounded browser
   retention and playback, and keeps its parser/reducer headlessly testable.
3. Keep the existing native graphics path as an optional second renderer for
   desktop/3-D views, sharing the same observation contract. Request `sw-mlpl`
   changes only where its server or protocol demonstrably blocks the Yew host;
   do not add a duplicate core Explorer speculatively.
4. Add side-by-side execution comparison only after stable observation names
   and retention policies are proven.

Exit: the Yew browser and optional native hosts visualize the same MLPL-authored data
without knowing which algorithm produced it.

## Cross-cutting gates

- Every executable behavior starts with native mlplunit coverage and focused
  probes; `just check` is the full precommit gate.
- Every `.mlpl` file has a module comment, every user function has a first-body
  docstring, and canonical formatting is checked before commit and push.
- Lessons are deterministic and bounded; large values fail visibly until an
  explicit full/sample/summary policy is specified.
- Documentation, catalog, capability ledger, static fallback, and acceptance
  evidence change with the behavior they describe.
- Sibling repositories remain read-only. Their work is documented as a
  handoff, not simulated through edits or undocumented checkout dependencies.

## Non-goals

- Reverse interpreter execution in the initial implementation.
- A dashboard-layout DSL before real lessons require one.
- Silent sampling or downsampling.
- A special-purpose GPT, attention, PCA, K-means, or optimizer renderer.
- A new package mechanism or duplicate MLPL library implementation here.
- Modifying any sibling repository from this saga.

# ML microscope delivery plan

## Outcome

Build executable sw-MLPL lessons whose own semantically named intermediate
values form a recorded, inspectable timeline. A learner can read and modify the
MLPL algorithm, rerun it, and review how its state changes without a bespoke
Rust implementation of each ML concept.

MLPL owns concepts and application semantics. Hosts render generic observed
values and manage playback or interaction. Work moves upstream only after a
downstream executable probe proves that current public behavior blocks a
general contract.

## Evidence and current constraints

- `emit_frame(name, step, x)` streams a whole numeric tensor through the
  connect-mode metric sink, returns `x`, and is a no-op when disconnected.
- sw-MLPL already provides arrays, named axes, autograd, model helpers,
  attention extraction, traces, SVG plots, browser/WASM execution, and SSE.
- Current frame events carry a name, numeric step, shape, and numeric values;
  they do not yet constitute a versioned multi-observation lesson protocol.
- `demo-extensions` already proves arrays, records, handles, a parked-main
  Port architecture, and headless/native rendering tests.
- `demo-mlpl-libraries` already proves revision-pinned, hash-verified source
  vendoring for reusable MLPL modules.
- Recorded rewind is host-side browsing. Reverse evaluation and synchronous
  browser checkpoints are deliberately outside the first milestone.

## Architecture rule

```text
demo-ml-microscope (.mlpl concepts and lessons)
          |
          +-- repeated domain-neutral helpers --> demo-mlpl-libraries
          |
          +-- generic native UI requirement ----> demo-extensions (Rust)
          |
          `-- proven language-wide blocker ------> sw-mlpl
```

Rust may define generic observation envelopes, bounded retention, tensor
inspectors, renderers, timelines, transports, and playback controls. It must
not define `TransformerVisualizer`, `PcaVisualizer`, `KMeansVisualizer`, or
other algorithm-specific semantics.

## Saga 1: foundation and measured contract

1. Establish Agentrail instructions, licensing, project README, repository
   checks, architecture, cross-repository ownership, and an evidence-backed
   capability ledger.
2. Probe `emit_frame` across the supported interpreter/connect path and freeze
   the smallest recorded-observation contract: names, steps, grouping, numeric
   shapes, fidelity, ordering, budgets, errors, and disconnected behavior.
3. Add root mlplunit/tool selection/style infrastructure and one tiny fixture
   proving the current public API without adding Rust or changing siblings.

Exit: `just check` passes from a clean checkout and documentation distinguishes
supported, awkward, and blocked behavior using executable evidence.

## Saga 2: pure-MLPL proof of concept

After the first two lessons, prioritize the implementation-ready Rust/Yew
viewer handoff so interactive playback can proceed in `demo-extensions` before
the K-means lesson. This ordering change does not authorize sibling edits from
this repository.

1. Implement matrix multiplication as concept stepping: inputs, selected row
   and column, products, partial sums, and completed output.
2. Implement two-parameter linear regression/gradient descent with data,
   predictions, residuals, loss, gradients, parameters, and trajectory frames.
3. Implement K-means with explicit initial, assignment, and centroid-update
   phases, forcing a clean convention for multiple observations per step.
4. Build a deterministic recorded-timeline artifact and a dependency-free
   textual/static viewer sufficient for acceptance; browser and native hosts
   remain optional consumers of the same data.

Exit: three unrelated lessons use the same small observation helpers; retained
state is bounded; numeric/text evidence exists independently of visuals.

## Saga 3: reusable MLPL observation library

1. Review the helpers after three consumers and freeze only domain-neutral
   functions such as observe-at, metric, note, and bounded summaries.
2. Write a producer contract and a separately actionable extraction handoff for
   `demo-mlpl-libraries`, including prefixes, tests, catalog metadata, install
   provenance, and migration order.
3. After that sibling change is independently delivered, vendor the immutable
   library revision here and prove hash-checked consumption. Do not couple this
   repo to an adjacent working tree at runtime.

Exit: this repository consumes a pinned library; lesson semantics remain local.

## Saga 4: deeper ML learning path

Add capability-supported lessons in prerequisite order: vector/shape
inspection, MLP forward pass, explicit backward gradients, PCA, attention,
tiny language model, LoRA, and Engram. Each lesson names shapes, tolerance,
claim boundaries, and the exact supported/awkward/blocking capabilities it
exercises. Transformer work reuses sw-MLPL's model implementation; it does not
implement a second transformer in Rust.

Exit: the learning path reaches a small real model while remaining readable,
bounded, deterministic, and executable as MLPL.

## Saga 5: generic hosts after protocol proof

1. Specify a versioned, renderer-neutral observation/timeline interchange from
   measured artifacts, including budgets and malformed-input behavior.
2. Hand off a full-featured generic Rust/Yew WASM microscope to
   `demo-extensions`. It consumes ordered SSE frames, owns bounded browser
   retention and playback, and keeps its parser/reducer headlessly testable.
3. Keep the existing native graphics path as an optional second renderer for
   desktop/3-D views, sharing the same observation contract. Request `sw-mlpl`
   changes only where its server or protocol demonstrably blocks the Yew host;
   do not add a duplicate core Explorer speculatively.
4. Add side-by-side execution comparison only after stable observation names
   and retention policies are proven.

Exit: the Yew browser and optional native hosts visualize the same MLPL-authored data
without knowing which algorithm produced it.

## Cross-cutting gates

- Every executable behavior starts with native mlplunit coverage and focused
  probes; `just check` is the full precommit gate.
- Every `.mlpl` file has a module comment, every user function has a first-body
  docstring, and canonical formatting is checked before commit and push.
- Lessons are deterministic and bounded; large values fail visibly until an
  explicit full/sample/summary policy is specified.
- Documentation, catalog, capability ledger, static fallback, and acceptance
  evidence change with the behavior they describe.
- Sibling repositories remain read-only. Their work is documented as a
  handoff, not simulated through edits or undocumented checkout dependencies.

## Non-goals

- Reverse interpreter execution in the initial implementation.
- A dashboard-layout DSL before real lessons require one.
- Silent sampling or downsampling.
- A special-purpose GPT, attention, PCA, K-means, or optimizer renderer.
- A new package mechanism or duplicate MLPL library implementation here.
- Modifying any sibling repository from this saga.

<!-- AUTOGENERATED BY `agentrail instructions apply` — DO NOT EDIT BY HAND -->

## Baseline expectations for agentrail-driven sessions

You are working with the agentrail saga/steps process. The saga record (the
`.agentrail/` directory) is the durable handoff between sessions — if your
work is not reflected there, the next session cannot see it.

Before reporting work as complete:

- Confirm the active step is reflected in `.agentrail/` and committed.
- Run the project's pre-commit gate (tests, lint, format) before
  `agentrail complete`, not after.
- If you discover unplanned work, prefer `agentrail insert` / `agentrail add`
  over silently doing it inside another step.

## CRITICAL: Agentrail session protocol (follow exactly)

Every session follows this sequence. Do not skip steps, do not reorder.

### 1. START — `agentrail next`
First thing in the session. Read the output carefully: it tells you the
current step number, prompt, skill docs, and past trajectories. If `next`
exits non-zero, the saga is complete or absent — do not invent work.

### 2. BEGIN — `agentrail begin`
Run immediately after reading `next` output. This transitions the step from
Pending to InProgress so the recorded history matches what actually
happened.

### 3. WORK
Do what the step prompt says. Do NOT ask the user "want me to proceed?" or
"shall I start?" — the step prompt IS your instruction. Execute it.

### 4. COMMIT
Commit your code changes with git BEFORE running `agentrail complete`.
The commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at
the moment of `complete`, so the commit must land first.

### 5. COMPLETE — `agentrail complete`
```
agentrail complete --summary "what you accomplished" \
  --reward 1 \
  --actions "tools and approach used"
```
On failure: `--reward -1 --failure-mode "what went wrong"`.
On final step: add `--done`.

### 6. STOP
After `complete`, do NOT make further code changes. Anything after
`complete` is untracked and invisible to the next session. If you see more
work to do, it belongs in the NEXT step, not this one.

## Agentrail metadata discipline

When using agentrail, changes to `.agentrail/` files are first-class project
changes — the same as application source code. They must be committed, and
should be pushed before you hand off.

Before running `agentrail complete`:

1. `git status` — confirm `.agentrail/` files are tracked, not just present.
   Untracked files in `.agentrail/` mean the next session will not see them.
2. Stage and commit source changes and `.agentrail/` metadata together. The
   commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at the
   moment of `agentrail complete`, so the commit must happen *first*.
3. Run `agentrail complete` after the commit lands.
4. Push the branch (or note the unpushed branch state in your handoff).

This is the most common agentrail failure mode: agents do the work, commit
the source, and forget the `.agentrail/` files. The result is a saga whose
recorded history disagrees with git history, which `agentrail audit` will
flag — but only after the damage is done.

### What's hand-editable in `.agentrail/`

Three categories of files live here, and the rules differ:

- **Append-only saga state** — `saga.toml`, `step.toml`, `plan.md`, session
  JSONLs under `sessions/`, trajectory JSONs under `trajectories/`, and
  anything under `.agentrail-archive/`. **Never hand-edit or delete these.**
  They are written by agentrail commands and represent the durable saga
  record; hand-editing desyncs the saga from git history and from prior
  session memory. A direct `rm` on untracked files is unrecoverable.
- **Regenerated state** — `instruction-lock.toml`. Don't hand-edit; it is
  rewritten on every `agentrail instructions apply`, so any local changes
  are overwritten silently.
- **User config** — `instruction-profile.toml`. This is normal user-edited
  config, like `.gitconfig` or a `package.json`. Hand-edit it freely, or
  use `agentrail instructions profile *` subcommands to mutate via
  commands (which validate field values and surface typos).

## Branch handoff after `agentrail complete`

Once a feature branch is committed and `agentrail complete` has run,
signal that it is ready for review/merge by renaming it from
`feat/<slug>` to `pr/<slug>`:

```bash
git branch -m feat/<slug> pr/<slug>
```

The rename is a useful convention regardless of how this project
handles handoff:

- It distinguishes "in-progress work" from "awaiting review" in the
  output of `git branch`.
- Project-specific tooling (CI, release-engineer scans, automated PR
  creation) can key off the `pr/*` prefix.
- It keeps the branch name stable across the review cycle even if the
  feature slug evolves.

What happens after the rename depends on what push capability you
have. See `push-discipline.md` for how to detect capability before
trying.

- **You can push and use GitHub PRs.** Push the renamed branch and
  open the PR:
  ```bash
  git push -u origin pr/<slug>
  gh pr create
  ```
  (Or push and open the PR via the web UI.)
- **You cloned via HTTPS without push access to the upstream remote.**
  Typical when contributing to an open-source project you don't own:
  push the renamed branch to your fork instead, then open the PR
  pointing at upstream. `git remote -v` shows your remotes; add a
  fork remote with `git remote add fork <url>` if needed.
- **Your project has a project-specific handoff flow** (release
  engineer scanning for `pr/*` branches, automated PR creation, CI
  hooks). The rename IS the handoff signal. Look for site-specific
  guidance in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md outside the briefing markers — if
  present, follow that instead.

After the rename, do not continue committing to `pr/<slug>` — those
commits will not be in the PR. Start further work on a fresh branch
off the (eventually merged and pulled) base.

## Push discipline

When you push (typically after `branch-handoff` has renamed `feat/X`
to `pr/X` and you're publishing the PR branch), do it safely.

### Verify push capability before assuming it works

- `git remote get-url origin` — `git@…` (SSH) or `https://…` plus a
  configured credential helper is push-capable. A bare `https://…`
  with no helper usually is not (read-only mirror or fresh clone).
- `gh auth status` — if the project uses GitHub PRs and `gh` is not
  authenticated, `gh pr create` will fail.
- `git push --dry-run` — surfaces auth or branch-protection problems
  without changing remote state.

### If you cannot push (or push fails)

- Note the unpushed branch state explicitly in your `agentrail
  complete --summary` so the next session knows the work is local.
- Do NOT silently leave commits stranded on a local branch — the next
  agent will look at the remote and assume your work was lost.
- Do NOT retry the same `git push` in a loop. If the failure is a
  permission issue (no SSH key, no `gh` auth, sandboxed user), retries
  will not fix it. Surface the failure to the user.
- If this project has a project-specific handoff flow (release
  engineer scans for `pr/*` branches, queue files, CI hooks
  documented in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md outside the briefing markers),
  follow that instead of pushing — the branch rename from
  `branch-handoff.md` may already be sufficient.

### If the remote rejects a push

- For non-fast-forward errors on a personal branch, prefer
  `git pull --rebase` over `--force` unless the user has explicitly
  authorized force-push.
- Never force-push to a shared branch (`main`, release branches)
  without an explicit instruction.
- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared
  branch.

## Recovery: detecting and repairing saga/git drift

The saga is a record of git history. When the two diverge — agent forgets
to commit `.agentrail/`, a step is reverted, files are renamed by hand —
agentrail provides two recovery tools.

### `agentrail audit`

Compares first-parent git history against saga steps and reports gaps.
Default output is a markdown report; `--emit-commands` prints a shell
script of `agentrail add` lines pre-seeded from commit subjects:

```bash
agentrail audit                    # human-readable report
agentrail audit --emit-commands    # draft script (review before running)
agentrail audit --since HEAD~50    # limit scope
```

The emitted script is a draft — slugs and prompts come from commit
subjects and usually need rewording. Review and edit before executing.

### `agentrail snapshot` (belt-and-suspenders)

Captures `.agentrail/` (and `.agentrail-archive/` if present) into a real
git commit under `refs/agentrail/snapshots/<timestamp>`. The blobs are
reachable, survive `git gc`, and can be restored with a normal git
command:

```bash
agentrail snapshot                 # take a snapshot now
agentrail snapshot --list          # list existing refs
git restore --source=<ref> -- .agentrail .agentrail-archive
```

Run a snapshot before risky agent operations or after creating files
you haven't yet staged. It does NOT replace normal git tracking — it is
a safety net for what is not yet committed.

## Git hygiene

- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch.
- Never use `--no-verify` to skip pre-commit hooks unless explicitly told to.
  If a hook fails, fix the underlying issue.
- Prefer naming files explicitly (`git add path/to/file`) over `git add -A`,
  to avoid sweeping in unintended files (secrets, local scratch, etc.).
- Resolve merge conflicts; do not discard changes by default.

<!-- agentrail:global:end -->

This repository uses Agentrail sagas and `AGENTS.md` as its single instruction
source. Do not create a duplicate `CLAUDE.md`.

## Repository policy

- Work directly on `main`; do not create feature branches or pull requests.
- Follow `agentrail next`, `agentrail begin`, work, test, commit,
  `agentrail complete`, then stop. Never hand-edit Agentrail-managed state.
- Commit source, documentation, tests, and durable `.agentrail/` state together
  before completing a step. Stage named files, never broad worktree sweeps.
- Treat every sibling repository as read-only. Record separately actionable
  work in the appropriate handoff document; never change a sibling from here.
- Never install or overwrite stable user tools. Prefer explicit absolute tool
  overrides, then `PATH`, then documented adjacent development checkouts.

## MLPL microscope contract

- MLPL owns ML concepts, lesson order, observations, annotations, and
  application semantics. Rust hosts may own only generic rendering, transport,
  storage, lifecycle, and interaction primitives.
- Start with recorded playback over current public sw-MLPL behavior. Rewind
  means browsing retained observations, not reversing interpreter execution.
- Use `emit_frame` as the initial low-level observation primitive and return
  observed values unchanged through MLPL helpers. Do not request new upstream
  syntax or builtins until executable probes demonstrate a blocking gap.
- Keep lessons deterministic, bounded, standalone, self-explaining, and honest
  about which work runs in MLPL, a native extension, or the host.
- Visuals are evidence. Every lesson must include textual/numeric evidence and
  explain shapes, tolerances, prerequisites, its exact claim, and what its
  finite fixture does not prove.
- Promote helpers to `../demo-mlpl-libraries` only after at least three
  unrelated lessons prove a stable, domain-neutral API. Put generic native
  viewer experiments in `../demo-extensions`; keep algorithm-specific Rust
  types out of that handoff.
- Classify language findings as supported, awkward-but-expressible, or
  blocking. A blocker needs a minimal probe, required semantics, acceptance
  cases, affected lessons, and an honest unavailable status.

## Testing and completion gate

- Use test-driven development for executable behavior. MLPL behavior requires
  native mlplunit tests with root `mlplunit.conf`, `tests/test_*.mlpl`, `@test`
  registration, shared assertions, and one `u:run_registered_tests()` call.
- Every tracked `.mlpl` file starts with a module-purpose comment; every
  user-defined function has a first-expression docstring; canonical formatting
  is mandatory.
- Use a root `justfile` as the entry point and keep recipes thin. Portable work
  belongs in `scripts/`; do not add Makefiles.
- Before every commit and push, run `scripts/check-mlpl-style` and `just check`.
  The full gate must include documentation/structure checks, executable probes,
  demos, and mlplunit once those artifacts exist. `sw-checklist` applies only
  to Rust work in `../demo-extensions`, not to this MLPL repository.
- Update README, architecture, lesson catalog, capability ledger, handoffs, and
  acceptance evidence in the same step as affected behavior.
- Inspect `.gitignore` and `git status --short`, stage named paths, commit on
  `main`, push with `git push origin main`, and verify success before reporting
  completion. Never force-push or bypass hooks.
- Run `agentrail complete` only after the implementation commit and successful
  gate. If completion changes durable metadata, commit and push those exact
  files separately, then make no further source changes.
- At the end of every Agentrail step, summarize what was completed, checks run,
  commit/push status, what the next step will deliver, and explicit blockers or
  limitations (`none` when there are none).

Planning references: `docs/research.txt`, `docs/architecture.md`,
`docs/plan.md`, `docs/sagas.md`, `docs/cross-repo-handoffs.md`, and
`docs/sw-mlpl-blockers.md`.

- **User config** — `instruction-profile.toml`. This is normal user-edited
  config, like `.gitconfig` or a `package.json`. Hand-edit it freely, or
  use `agentrail instructions profile *` subcommands to mutate via
  commands (which validate field values and surface typos).

## Branch handoff after `agentrail complete`

Once a feature branch is committed and `agentrail complete` has run,
signal that it is ready for review/merge by renaming it from
`feat/<slug>` to `pr/<slug>`:

```bash
git branch -m feat/<slug> pr/<slug>
```

The rename is a useful convention regardless of how this project
handles handoff:

- It distinguishes "in-progress work" from "awaiting review" in the
  output of `git branch`.
- Project-specific tooling (CI, release-engineer scans, automated PR
  creation) can key off the `pr/*` prefix.
- It keeps the branch name stable across the review cycle even if the
  feature slug evolves.

What happens after the rename depends on what push capability you
have. See `push-discipline.md` for how to detect capability before
trying.

- **You can push and use GitHub PRs.** Push the renamed branch and
  open the PR:
  ```bash
  git push -u origin pr/<slug>
  gh pr create
  ```
  (Or push and open the PR via the web UI.)
- **You cloned via HTTPS without push access to the upstream remote.**
  Typical when contributing to an open-source project you don't own:
  push the renamed branch to your fork instead, then open the PR
  pointing at upstream. `git remote -v` shows your remotes; add a
  fork remote with `git remote add fork <url>` if needed.
- **Your project has a project-specific handoff flow** (release
  engineer scanning for `pr/*` branches, automated PR creation, CI
  hooks). The rename IS the handoff signal. Look for site-specific
  guidance in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md outside the briefing markers — if
  present, follow that instead.

After the rename, do not continue committing to `pr/<slug>` — those
commits will not be in the PR. Start further work on a fresh branch
off the (eventually merged and pulled) base.

## Push discipline

When you push (typically after `branch-handoff` has renamed `feat/X`
to `pr/X` and you're publishing the PR branch), do it safely.

### Verify push capability before assuming it works

- `git remote get-url origin` — `git@…` (SSH) or `https://…` plus a
  configured credential helper is push-capable. A bare `https://…`
  with no helper usually is not (read-only mirror or fresh clone).
- `gh auth status` — if the project uses GitHub PRs and `gh` is not
  authenticated, `gh pr create` will fail.
- `git push --dry-run` — surfaces auth or branch-protection problems
  without changing remote state.

### If you cannot push (or push fails)

- Note the unpushed branch state explicitly in your `agentrail
  complete --summary` so the next session knows the work is local.
- Do NOT silently leave commits stranded on a local branch — the next
  agent will look at the remote and assume your work was lost.
- Do NOT retry the same `git push` in a loop. If the failure is a
  permission issue (no SSH key, no `gh` auth, sandboxed user), retries
  will not fix it. Surface the failure to the user.
- If this project has a project-specific handoff flow (release
  engineer scans for `pr/*` branches, queue files, CI hooks
  documented in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md outside the briefing markers),
  follow that instead of pushing — the branch rename from
  `branch-handoff.md` may already be sufficient.

### If the remote rejects a push

- For non-fast-forward errors on a personal branch, prefer
  `git pull --rebase` over `--force` unless the user has explicitly
  authorized force-push.
- Never force-push to a shared branch (`main`, release branches)
  without an explicit instruction.
- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared
  branch.

## Recovery: detecting and repairing saga/git drift

The saga is a record of git history. When the two diverge — agent forgets
to commit `.agentrail/`, a step is reverted, files are renamed by hand —
agentrail provides two recovery tools.

### `agentrail audit`

Compares first-parent git history against saga steps and reports gaps.
Default output is a markdown report; `--emit-commands` prints a shell
script of `agentrail add` lines pre-seeded from commit subjects:

```bash
agentrail audit                    # human-readable report
agentrail audit --emit-commands    # draft script (review before running)
agentrail audit --since HEAD~50    # limit scope
```

The emitted script is a draft — slugs and prompts come from commit
subjects and usually need rewording. Review and edit before executing.

### `agentrail snapshot` (belt-and-suspenders)

Captures `.agentrail/` (and `.agentrail-archive/` if present) into a real
git commit under `refs/agentrail/snapshots/<timestamp>`. The blobs are
reachable, survive `git gc`, and can be restored with a normal git
command:

```bash
agentrail snapshot                 # take a snapshot now
agentrail snapshot --list          # list existing refs
git restore --source=<ref> -- .agentrail .agentrail-archive
```

Run a snapshot before risky agent operations or after creating files
you haven't yet staged. It does NOT replace normal git tracking — it is
a safety net for what is not yet committed.

## Git hygiene

- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch.
- Never use `--no-verify` to skip pre-commit hooks unless explicitly told to.
  If a hook fails, fix the underlying issue.
- Prefer naming files explicitly (`git add path/to/file`) over `git add -A`,
  to avoid sweeping in unintended files (secrets, local scratch, etc.).
- Resolve merge conflicts; do not discard changes by default.

<!-- agentrail:global:end -->

This repository uses Agentrail sagas and `AGENTS.md` as its single instruction
source. Do not create a duplicate `CLAUDE.md`.

## Repository policy

- Work directly on `main`; do not create feature branches or pull requests.
- Follow `agentrail next`, `agentrail begin`, work, test, commit,
  `agentrail complete`, then stop. Never hand-edit Agentrail-managed state.
- Commit source, documentation, tests, and durable `.agentrail/` state together
  before completing a step. Stage named files, never broad worktree sweeps.
- Treat every sibling repository as read-only. Record separately actionable
  work in the appropriate handoff document; never change a sibling from here.
- Never install or overwrite stable user tools. Prefer explicit absolute tool
  overrides, then `PATH`, then documented adjacent development checkouts.

## MLPL microscope contract

- MLPL owns ML concepts, lesson order, observations, annotations, and
  application semantics. Rust hosts may own only generic rendering, transport,
  storage, lifecycle, and interaction primitives.
- Start with recorded playback over current public sw-MLPL behavior. Rewind
  means browsing retained observations, not reversing interpreter execution.
- Use `emit_frame` as the initial low-level observation primitive and return
  observed values unchanged through MLPL helpers. Do not request new upstream
  syntax or builtins until executable probes demonstrate a blocking gap.
- Keep lessons deterministic, bounded, standalone, self-explaining, and honest
  about which work runs in MLPL, a native extension, or the host.
- Visuals are evidence. Every lesson must include textual/numeric evidence and
  explain shapes, tolerances, prerequisites, its exact claim, and what its
  finite fixture does not prove.
- Promote helpers to `../demo-mlpl-libraries` only after at least three
  unrelated lessons prove a stable, domain-neutral API. Put generic native
  viewer experiments in `../demo-extensions`; keep algorithm-specific Rust
  types out of that handoff.
- Classify language findings as supported, awkward-but-expressible, or
  blocking. A blocker needs a minimal probe, required semantics, acceptance
  cases, affected lessons, and an honest unavailable status.

## Testing and completion gate

- Use test-driven development for executable behavior. MLPL behavior requires
  native mlplunit tests with root `mlplunit.conf`, `tests/test_*.mlpl`, `@test`
  registration, shared assertions, and one `u:run_registered_tests()` call.
- Every tracked `.mlpl` file starts with a module-purpose comment; every
  user-defined function has a first-expression docstring; canonical formatting
  is mandatory.
- Use a root `justfile` as the entry point and keep recipes thin. Portable work
  belongs in `scripts/`; do not add Makefiles.
- Before every commit and push, run `scripts/check-mlpl-style` and `just check`.
  The full gate must include documentation/structure checks, executable probes,
  demos, and mlplunit once those artifacts exist. `sw-checklist` applies only
  to Rust work in `../demo-extensions`, not to this MLPL repository.
- Update README, architecture, lesson catalog, capability ledger, handoffs, and
  acceptance evidence in the same step as affected behavior.
- Inspect `.gitignore` and `git status --short`, stage named paths, commit on
  `main`, push with `git push origin main`, and verify success before reporting
  completion. Never force-push or bypass hooks.
- Run `agentrail complete` only after the implementation commit and successful
  gate. If completion changes durable metadata, commit and push those exact
  files separately, then make no further source changes.
- At the end of every Agentrail step, summarize what was completed, checks run,
  commit/push status, what the next step will deliver, and explicit blockers or
  limitations (`none` when there are none).
